To solve this, we are announcing the General Availability (GA) of the AlloyDB Omni Web UI for Red Hat and containers . This production-ready, read-only console gives you direct visibility into hardware telemetry, query performance, and configuration flags for AlloyDB Omni so you can troubleshoot workloads quickly and safely without leaving your local or enterprise environment. What is AlloyDB Omni? AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, self-managed edition of AlloyDB that brings enterprise capabilities and full PostgreSQL compatibility to your own infrastructure. Built to run anywhere — across on-premises data centers, edge environments, and multi-cloud deployments — it includes built-in columnar acceleration and integrated AI tooling. With AlloyDB Omni, you can modernize demanding transactional and analytical workloads while retaining complete control over your operating environment. Key Web UI capabilities at a glance Cluster overview and profiles: Switch between target connection profiles quickly without using the command line. System monitoring: View real-time performance telemetry for CPU, memory, and disk I/O to plan capacity and triage infrastructure issues. Query performance: Identify resource-heavy SQL statements through a visual breakdown of database load, latency bottlenecks, and slow queries. Columnar Engine diagnostics: Track the in-memory columnar store, caching, and coverage to verify analytical query acceleration. Parameter and flag auditing: Inspect runtime database parameters centrally to identify configuration drift against your organizational baselines. AlloyDB AI and ecosystem shortcuts: Inspect vector search and AI workflows, and access quick launchpad shortcuts for ecosystem tools like pgBackRest. Read-only operations: The interface operates strictly in read-only mode, ensuring that diagnostic sessions cannot execute write commands or modify your underlying database configurations. Dual-layer observability: System and query monitoring To isolate production performance spikes, you need immediate visibility into both hardware health and SQL statement execution. System monitoring: The Web UI integrates with standard Prometheus telemetry to show you real-time CPU use, memory allocation, storage I/O, and active connection trends. Query monitoring: The dashboard automatically ranks execution-heavy SQL statements by total latency and call frequency. You can instantly isolate unindexed or resource-intensive queries to resolve issues faster. title: Near-zero downtime upgrades: Announcing Cloud SQL for MySQL blue-green deployments
raw_text:
Keeping production databases on supported versions shouldn’t require giving up your weekend. To stay secure, compliant, and with the best performance and newest AI capabilities, organizations need to run on the latest database engine versions. Yet for many teams, major version upgrades mean weeks of cross-team coordination, negotiating narrow maintenance windows, and hours of application downtime. In an era where mission-critical applications and AI agents operate as 24/7 systems of action, even a brief maintenance outage can mean disrupted customer experiences and lost revenue. To help, we are excited to announce the preview of fully managed blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL , starting with Cloud SQL for MySQL. You can now execute major version upgrades and configuration updates with minimal downtime via the Google Cloud console or automated CLI scripts. By continuously synchronizing a parallel environment, teams can safely test with production data before a seamless cutover — all while keeping the original database as a reliable safety net after the switchover. Why the upgrade dilemma matters to your business Putting off major version upgrades (like moving from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4) exposes you to security vulnerabilities and causes you to miss out on performance improvements and latest AI capabilities. To test changes and avoid in-place upgrade downtime, teams often turn to a blue-green deployment — testing changes on a separate, upgraded staging copy (green) alongside the live database (blue) and switching traffic over once it’s ready. However, manual blue-green setups are incredibly complex to build, synchronize, and safely cut over. Cloud SQL’s fully managed blue-green deployments can turn your database upgrades from a high-risk weekend project into a predictable, low-downtime operation. The traditional upgrade The managed blue-green way Late-night maintenance: Scheduling hours of offline downtime at 2:00 AM on a Saturday. Business-hour upgrades: Staging, sync, and testing happen in the background during normal work hours. Limited testing options : Tests are limited to non-production environments, adding operational risks. Pre-cutover verification: Safely testing actual applications against real-time production data copy before any traffic shifts. High-stress rollbacks: If an issue is found, rebuilding or restoring from backups takes hours. Built-in fallback: Cancel the upgrade and leave your blue instance as is if issues come up, or keep your “old blue” as a manual fallback after cutover. The technical differentiators With Cloud SQL, managed blue-green deployments automate the entire lifecycle across three stages: Blue environment (production): Your current primary Cloud SQL instance, which continues serving live application traffic without interruption. Green environment (staging): A temporary clone of your blue instance that Cloud SQL upgrades to your target database version and keeps in sync via continuous replication. Switchover: When you're ready to cut over, Cloud SQL briefly sets the blue instance to read-only, finishes the final data synchronization, and promotes the green instance to your new primary database. Three notable capabilities make this release a game-changer for enterprise workloads: Near-zero downtime cutover: The transition from the old version to the new version is incredibly fast. Organizations using Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus experience sub-second downtime for maintenance . No application changes: When you trigger the switchover, Cloud SQL automatically transfers your existing database IP address, instance name, and backups to the new database. Your developers do not need to rewrite connection strings, modify configuration files, or update client applications. Safe, real-data testing: You can run real application traffic and queries against the upgraded green environment to verify performance before going live. If you spot an issue, simply delete the deployment before switchover without touching your live database. Simple to orchestrate, built to scale Upgrading your database environment can now be initiated in just a few clicks within the console, or via a simple CLI script. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "# Create the synchronized, upgraded green deployment environment

# Check the status and get the test endpoint
gcloud sql blue-green-deployments describe my-upgrade \
--region=us-central1

# Connect and test the upgraded copy
gcloud sql connect TARGET_INSTANCE_NAME --user=admin

# Switch your live traffic to the upgraded database in seconds
gcloud sql blue-green-deployments switchover my-upgrade

# Clean up the old database when you're ready
gcloud sql blue-green-deployments delete my-upgrade \

title: Behind the scenes, two months later: How we ship Google Agent Skills like products
raw_text:
In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills , covering how the project started, how we maintain quality at scale, and how we handle governance. In this post, I'll share what we've built since then: the automated quality gates that every change must pass, the AI review agent that inspects skill quality, and the lessons that we learned along the way. You can adopt similar gates and review rules in your own skill repository. Since my last post, the Google Agent Skills repository has passed 21,000 GitHub stars, up from 15,000. It now hosts over 170 skills from teams across Google, and we distribute them across multiple AI platforms. Building agent skills for a single developer or a small project is straightforward. You write a SKILL.md file, define a few instructions, test it manually, and it works. At our scale, manual workflows stop being effective. Unvetted edits can introduce subtle bugs, and it becomes difficult to catch issues before they reach users. The core philosophy: Ship skills like products One key lesson from my previous post: a skill is a living product, not a one-off document. In practice, that means we ship every skill update like a product release. It's tempting to treat a skill as documentation. But documentation explains concepts to a human reader, while a skill steers an AI agent's reasoning loop, tool selection, and execution path. A misplaced phrase in a skill can cause an agent to invoke invalid command flags, enter an infinite loop, or waste tokens. That makes every instruction edit a behavioral change. You wouldn't ship a product update without testing it, and the same goes for a skill. This principle drives three core requirements: Strict semantic versioning : Every behavioral change requires an explicit version bump. Deterministic automated validation : Linters and validators check every proposed change before a human or AI reviewer sees it. Mandatory evaluation evidence : Every change includes an evaluation report. It compares the skill against its previous version, or—if the skill is new—against an agent without the skill. Automated conformance gates: The pull request pipeline In my previous post, I briefly listed the checks that every skill passes on check-in: linters, link checkers, and AI-assisted checklists. Here's what's inside them, plus two gates that I haven't covered before: semantic versioning and evaluation suite validation. When an author submits a change to our internal skills repository, an automated continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline triggers immediately. Before a skill is exported to GitHub, it must pass these six automated gates and receive human approval: Structural conformance : Directory layout, allowed files, and taxonomy. Skill linters : Frontmatter, folder naming, and Markdown rules. Semantic versioning : Version bump for every behavioral change. Evaluation suite : Valid eval suite and a fresh eval report. Link validation : Links are valid. AI review agent : Skill quality and design standards. Human approval : Final approval from a human reviewer (a subject matter expert) . Structural conformance and skill linters Our automated validation suite inspects every pull request for structural and syntactical correctness. Some of the rules include these requirements: Folder name and metadata name must match. SKILL.md and description length limits are enforced. All required fields in the frontmatter metadata are present. Only a curated list of files and directories is allowed within a skill directory. All Markdown files follow formatting rules. The main README.md file and the machine-readable index.json registry are up to date. Semantic versioning Every skill declares a semantic version in its SKILL.md frontmatter metadata: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '---
name: spanner-basics
metadata:
 version: "1.1.1"
 category: Databases
description: ...
---'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2519f26650>)])]> First, our automated checks verify that the version is a quoted string. YAML parses unquoted values like 2.0 as numbers, which causes unexpected parsing errors in tools that expect a string. Second, the validator checks the version transition itself. New skills must start at 1.0.0 , and any change to an existing skill's instructions, scripts, or references requires a version bump or the pull request is blocked. Standard reset rules apply: bumping MAJOR (for example, 1.4.2 to 2.0.0 ) resets MINOR and PATCH to 0 , and bumping MINOR (for example, 1.4.2 to 1.5.0 ) resets PATCH to 0 . Why enforce strict versioning if the agent only reads the Markdown instructions? The version number is for the developer and their package tooling, not for the model at runtime. Skills don't auto-update in the background, which means there's no network check or latency overhead each time an agent invokes a skill. Instead, explicit versions let developers compare their locally installed skills against the upstream catalog and decide when to pull changes—for example, by running the npx skills update command. This versioning also supports workflows where teams want to lock a critical skill to a known-good version to guarantee reproducible agent behavior across their projects. Evaluation suite validation Our continuous evaluations (evals) compare agent performance with and without each skill. Those results are only as reliable as the evaluation suites behind them. If a suite contains broken file references or compound expectations, test results become noisy and untrustworthy. Our validator parses each evaluation suite and the pull request description. Then it checks several strict invariants: Resolution of file-based prompts : When a test prompt references a file (such as @file:test_prompt.txt ), the validator confirms that the target file exists and that it isn't empty. Atomic expectations : Each expectation must check exactly one criterion. The validator blocks compound expectations until authors split them. Lesson 2 later in this post shows why. Duplicate detection : The validator flags duplicate test prompts and conflicting expectations within the same evaluation suite. Mandatory evaluation report : Every pull request that modifies a skill must link to an evaluation report in its description. Eval staleness check : Authors usually iterate on a pull request as reviewers leave feedback. The validator confirms that the linked report ran against the latest commit. Link validation Over 170 skills link to documentation for fast-evolving Google products, and those pages can move long after a skill passes review. Rather than waiting for users to report broken links, we validate links at two stages. Before merge, pull request checks verify all relative links, such as files in references/ . Then, every Monday, a GitHub Actions workflow runs lychee across all external links in the public repository and it reports any broken links to skill owners for remediation. AI review agent Linters and schema validators catch syntactic errors, but they can't evaluate overall quality. They can't tell you if an instruction is confusing, if a reference guide is too verbose, or if a task should have been a bash script instead of a large language model (LLM) instruction. To solve this, we integrated an AI review agent into our review pipeline. When a change affects a skill, the AI reviewer inspects it using a dedicated review skill. Yes, we use a skill to review skills. Here are the core rules the AI reviewer evaluates. You can adopt these rules in your own skill development workflows. 1. Skill suitability and the deterministic trap The first question our AI reviewer asks is simple: Does this task belong in an instruction? We often see authors fall into the deterministic trap . They write rigid, numbered sequences of command-line interface (CLI) commands directly into Markdown text. LLMs are probabilistic engines. If an operation requires a strict sequence of commands where a variation can cause an error, embedding those commands in the instruction text invites hallucinations. Our AI reviewer enforces a clear boundary between deterministic and probabilistic logic. Rigid CLI sequences, JSON parsers, and deployment steps must live in executable scripts under scripts/ . Markdown instructions are reserved for tasks that require judgment, such as choosing an architecture, diagnosing error logs, or synthesizing code. This rule complements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) guidance that I shared last time: prefer remote MCP tools whenever possible. When you must fall back to CLI or API calls, wrap them in a script instead of spelling them out in the instructions. 2. The L1/L2/L3 modular architecture Context windows are valuable. Loading a 2,000-line skill into an agent consumes context and degrades reasoning. Our AI reviewer enforces a three-tier information hierarchy that follows the progressive disclosure model of Agent Skills: Level 1 (Metadata) : The YAML frontmatter ( name , description ). The agent uses this concise summary for discovery and routing. Level 2 (Core instructions) : The main SKILL.md file. The body must stay compact (under 500 lines). It provides workflow overviews, decision trees, and guardrails. Level 3 (Reference docs) : Detailed API references, schemas, and other reference tables live in a references/ directory. Our AI reviewer enforces two distinct rules for Level 3: flat directory structure and single-hop indirection . Keeping references/ flat (no subdirectories) is a repository convention that discourages sprawling documentation trees and makes file discovery simpler. More importantly for runtime performance, the reviewer blocks chained references , where SKILL.md links to a reference file that links to yet another file. Each hop requires an extra tool call, adding latency and cost, and our evaluations showed that agents frequently stop before following a second level of chained references. 3. Non-interactive script design When skills bundle helper scripts in scripts/ , we expect agents to execute them directly in terminal sandboxes. Our AI reviewer flags any script that blocks on interactive prompts. Every script must accept inputs through command-line flags or environment variables, provide --help documentation, and include a --dry-run or confirmation flag for destructive operations. Scripts also need to separate output cleanly, writing structured data (usually JSON) to standard output and writing actionable error messages to standard error. Example AI review checklist snippet The review skill also checks frontmatter for spec compliance and discovery, and it turns the L1/L2/L3 architecture into concrete structure rules. Here's an excerpt from those criteria: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '### Front Matter & Discovery

- **Spec Compliance**: YAML front matter MUST strictly follow the Agent Skills
 Reference Specification (https://agentskills.io/specification). Use `>-`
 (folded strip-chomping) format for multi-line descriptions.
- **Description Quality**: The `description` field must follow the
 [Description Guide](references/description_guide.md).

### Content Structure & Authoring Quality

- **L1/L2/L3 Architecture**: Enforce modular structure. The main `SKILL.md`
 body must stay under 500 lines. Move deep domain reference material to
 `references/` (see [Skill Structure](references/skill_structure.md)).
- **Flat References Directory**: `references/` must be a flat directory (one
 level deep, no nested subdirectories). References > 100 lines must include a
 Table of Contents with line hints (see
 [Skill Structure](references/skill_structure.md)).
- **Avoid Deeply-Nested References**: Avoid deeply-nested references (e.g.,
 `SKILL.md` -> `references/guides.md` -> `assets/output.tmpl`). Keep
 reference structures shallow (one level of indirection from `SKILL.md`)
 because agents might not load such link targets fully.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f251a3e2950>)])]> Human approval After it passes all automated checks, every pull request must receive approval from a human reviewer. The reviewer is typically the skill's subject matter expert and, for new skills, a member of the Central Skills team. Lessons learned from repository history Six months of commit history and pull request discussions reveal several practical takeaways. 1. Scope CI checks carefully Early in the project, we configured automated pull request checks with broad directory patterns. One check required an approved bug tracking ticket on every change. Because the pattern matched too broadly, engineers making a one-line typo fix were blocked for missing a tracking ticket. Meanwhile, newly added skills in deeper subdirectories went uninspected. Takeaway : Match automated check rules to specific file operations, such as added versus modified files, and verify exact path depths. Treat minor edits to existing skills differently from new skills. 2. Atomic expectations When we started writing evaluation suites, we saw authors write compound expectations like this: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Bad: Compound expectation
- "The agent must create a Cloud Storage bucket in us-central1, enable
 uniform bucket-level access, and apply lifecycle rules."'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f251a0ceb10>)])]> If the agent configured the region and lifecycle rules but missed the uniform access flag, the LLM-as-a-judge scorer returned inconsistent ratings. Migrating to atomic expectations resolved the inconsistent ratings: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Good: Atomic expectations
- "The agent specifies us-central1 for the bucket location."
- "The agent enables uniform bucket-level access on the created bucket."
- "The agent defines a lifecycle configuration rule deleting objects
 older than 30 days."'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f251a3c6cd0>)])]> Takeaway : Check exactly one criterion per expectation. Atomic expectations make evaluation results clear, reliable, and debuggable. 3. Documentation drift happens fast In a multi-contributor repository, documentation tables drift within days if maintained manually. Takeaway : If you publish an index or catalog, never rely on contributors to update it manually. Instead, write a generator script and enforce it with a CI unit test. That's the origin of the README.md and index.json checks in our linters. Our index.json even opens with a warning: "This file is generated. Do not edit it by hand." 4. Gate expensive LLM checks behind fast deterministic ones Running full evaluation suites and an AI review agent on every change can get expensive fast, both in token usage and CI runtime—especially when authors push frequent small commits during review. In our pipeline, fast deterministic checks run first. Structural conformance, skill linters, and semantic versioning act as blocking gates: if any of them fail, the pipeline stops immediately and it won't trigger the AI reviewer or evaluation checks until those issues are fixed. Takeaway : Stage your pipeline so cheap, deterministic checks block broken changes before LLM-powered gates run. When you build a similar system, consider adding further cost guardrails, such as manual triggers for heavy checks (for example, a /run-evals pull request comment) or only triggering automatic re-runs when the diff exceeds a specific threshold. Conclusion Building a scalable Agent Skills repository requires more than good prompt engineering. It requires solid developer infrastructure: Ship skills like products: version, validate, and evaluate every change. Enforce semantic versioning and atomic expectations with automated CI gates. Use an AI reviewer to catch design anti-patterns, such as the deterministic trap. Check links before merge and on a schedule. Links and further reading To get started with Google Agent Skills, check out these resources: Google Agent Skills repo : github.com/google/skills Previous post : Behind the scenes: How we build, test, and scale Google Agent Skills Launch announcement : Level Up Your Agents: Announcing Google's Official Skills Repository Skills tutorial : Introduction: What Are Google Cloud Agent Skills? What's next? If you found this post helpful, share it with your friends on social media and connect with me on LinkedIn , X , or Bluesky . Thanks for reading!
summary: In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills , covering how the project started, how we maintain quality at scale, and how we handle governance. In this post, I'll share what we've built since then: the automated quality gates that every change must pass, the AI review agent that inspects skill quality, and the lessons that we learned along the way. You can adopt similar gates and review rules in your own skill repository. Since my last post, the Google Agent Skills repository has passed 21,000 GitHub stars, up from 15,000.

title: How to troubleshoot GKE workloads faster with VPC Flow Logs
raw_text: Having visibility into your network traffic is essential to operating Kubernetes environments effectively. When a service slows down or loses connectivity, knowing who is talking to whom lets you narrow the problem down quickly. In a standard cloud network, flow logs provide that view by recording connections between IP addresses, ports, and protocols. In Kubernetes, however, pods are temporary. Their IP addresses change constantly as pods scale, crash, or move between nodes, so a raw log entry showing 10.4.2.18 talking to 10.4.8.44 tells you little about which workload (and pod) owned that address, what namespace it was in, or what application it was trying to reach. By the time you search your cluster, the pod may already be gone! In a Google Cloud environment, VPC Flow Logs closes this gap at the network layer. Google Cloud's virtual network already sees every connection a pod makes, so each sampled flow is recorded with the Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) metadata behind the IP address: pod, workload, namespace, and service. You get workload-level attribution for L3/L4 traffic without deploying extra agents or sidecars, and it complements in-cluster Container Network Interface (CNI) and dataplane observability tools you may already run when you need deeper detail. Let’s take a deeper look at how VPC Flow Logs and GKE work together, and how to get started with it. How GKE metadata enriches VPC Flow Logs VPC Flow Logs samples traffic directly inside Google Cloud's virtual network. When flow logs are enabled for a subnet that hosts a GKE cluster, every record of pod traffic that passes through the VPC network is annotated with the Kubernetes context that owned the IP address at the time of sampling. This helps ensure the context is preserved even after the pod is gone: Cluster: The cluster name and location. Workload: The pod name and namespace, along with the controller that owns the pod, such as a deployment, StatefulSet, or DaemonSet. Service name: The Kubernetes service that received the traffic. Node and zone: The standard VPC fields, including the node VM and its zone on both ends of the flow. If you register your GKE workloads in App Hub , each record also carries application-level labels ( apphubSource and apphubDestination ) that identify the business application, environment, and criticality of each endpoint. This is especially useful when GKE microservices talk to App Hub-registered resources outside the cluster, such as Cloud Run services. Before you start Upgrade your log bucket to Observability Analytics (formerly Log Analytics): Flow Analyzer reads only from an upgraded bucket, typically _Default . Note: This upgrade is permanent. gcloud logging buckets update _Default \ --location=global \ --enable-analytics Enable VPC Flow Logs organization-wide: One organization-level configuration covers every subnet in every VPC network, including future clusters (requires Network Management Admin role). Keep include-all-metadata on so every record carries namespace and pod details. To balance visibility against cost, you can add a secondary sampling rate ( --flow-sampling ), an aggregation interval ( --aggregation-interval ), or a filter expression ( --filter-expr ) to view only the traffic of interest. gcloud network-management vpc-flow-logs-configs create CONFIG_NAME \ --location=global \ --organization=ORGANIZATION_ID \ --metadata=include-all-metadata Turn on intranode visibility : Autopilot clusters already have it, but you need to enable it on Standard clusters. Note: Enabling it restarts control plane and node components and adds some per-node overhead, so test it on a non-production cluster first. gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER_NAME \ --location=LOCATION \ --enable-intra-node-visibility Now you’re ready to get started. Analyze traffic visually in Flow Analyzer VPC Flow Logs write every record to Cloud Logging, you can search and query it in Logs Explorer or Log Analytics. For day-to-day work, Flow Analyzer , part of Network Intelligence Center, turns the same records into an interactive chart and table, so you can group and filter traffic by cluster, namespace, workload, pod, or service in a few clicks. The walkthroughs below use Online Boutique , an open-source microservices demo, on a GKE Autopilot cluster in us-central1. A loadgenerator deployment sends synthetic shopper traffic to the frontend , which calls productcatalogservice , cartservice , currencyservice , recommendationservice , shippingservice , adservice , and checkoutservice . Case 1: Turn IP addresses into workload names Whether you’re investigating an incident or assessing an architecture change, the first question is always the same: Which endpoints are communicating, and at what volume? Rather than presenting ephemeral IP address pairs, GKE metadata allows Flow Analyzer to answer this question directly using Kubernetes workload names. Steps in Flow Analyzer: Open Network Intelligence Center > Flow Analyzer and set the time range to last 1 hour . Under Source and Destination , set Organize flows by to GKE workload. In the filter bar, add the GKE workload is known filter so only pod-to-pod traffic is shown. Click Run new query . Grouping traffic by Source GKE workload and Destination GKE workload in Flow Analyzer to map microservice dependencies without raw IP lookups. Key insights: Sorted by volume, the table is a ready-made application dependency map: frontend handles incoming requests from loadgenerator (representing user traffic), while productcatalogservice answers calls from both recommendationservice and frontend . Because each row shows workload names instead of raw IP addresses, any unauthorized or unexpected workload-to-workload communication immediately becomes apparent. Case 2: Drill into a single service When a service is slow or about to change, you need to know who depends on it and how heavily. Steps in Flow Analyzer: Change Traffic aggregation to Client ↔ server (bidirectional) , so requests and responses between a pair are counted together. Under Server , add the filter GKE workload = productcatalogservice . Click Run new query , then click Details on the top row. Filtering on Server GKE workload (productcatalogservice) with Client ↔ server (bidirectional) aggregation to view caller share and the Details timeline. Key insights: You get every caller of the catalog service, each caller's share of its traffic, and a timeline for every pair, so if one caller's line climbs while the others stay flat, you know where to look first. When the question is latency rather than volume, switch the display mode to latency to rank the same callers by round-trip time. Case 3: Find the pods that talk across zones In a regional GKE cluster, chatty services that land in different zones send every request across a zone boundary, adding inter-zone data transfer charges. Because VPC Flow Logs record the zone at both ends of every flow, the pod pairs driving that traffic are easy to spot. Steps in Flow Analyzer: Switch from Basic filters to SQL filters , which let you compare two fields of the same flow. In the WHERE box, enter src_gcp_zone <> dest_gcp_zone . Set Organize flows by to Source GCP zone, Source GKE pod, Destination GCP zone , and Destination GKE pod . Click Run new query . Using SQL filters with src_gcp_zone <> dest_gcp_zone and multi-attribute grouping to identify pod pairs driving cross-zone network traffic. Key insights: The table displays cross-zone traffic ranked by volume, identifying the exact pods and zones on each end. In our cluster, the top flows occur between a frontend pod in us-central1-b and a currencyservice pod in us-central1-c, followed by checkoutservice , shippingservice , and productcatalogservice pairs. To investigate further, click Explore in Log Analytics to open the underlying SQL query for additional customization, such as adding joins or time buckets. GKE has a built-in answer: set trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone ( PreferClose on older versions) on the Service to prefer healthy endpoints in the caller's zone, and make sure each zone has enough replicas to serve its own traffic. What to keep in mind Pod-to-internet traffic: VPC Flow Logs carry no pod annotations, because the masquerade agent replaces the pod IP with the node IP before the flow is sampled. Keeping internal destinations in the non-masquerade list preserves pod names for those flows, and if you run ip-masq-agent with intranode visibility, that list must also include the cluster's node and pod IP ranges to avoid connectivity problems. Blocked traffic: Traffic blocked by a network policy never reaches the VPC network, so use NetworkPolicy logging to investigate it. Sampling: Flow logs are sampled, which makes byte and packet counts well suited for ranking and trending rather than per-connection accounting. Next steps If your clusters already have VPC Flow Logs turned on, upgrading the _Default bucket and opening Flow Analyzer is all it takes to reproduce the three walkthroughs above. title: How GKE networking scales to support high densities of concurrent AI agents
raw_text: What do you need to orchestrate high-density concurrent AI agents? As we transition from static requests toward autonomous agentic workflows, the need for secure, high-density sandboxes is pushing conventional infrastructure far beyond its architectural breaking point. This transition is driving top-tier research labs to demand infrastructure at unprecedented scale — often up to one million concurrent code-execution sandboxes! At this scale, the efficiency of your Kubernetes networking infrastructure directly impacts the economic viability of an agentic initiative. In advanced workflows like reinforcement learning (RL), extreme pod churn can mean thousands of isolated sandboxes spinning up and down every minute. To make sure that valuable GPUs and TPUs are spending their time executing models rather than waiting on sandboxes to initialize, you need sub-second provisioning and extreme compute density. By providing secure, lightweight isolation, Agent Sandbox on GKE is uniquely positioned to power these highly dynamic execution environments. Furthermore, for next-generation workloads with millions of concurrent idle sessions, Agent Substrate on GKE builds on these primitives to deliver even greater density and sub-second state rehydration. In this post, you will learn how GKE Dataplane V2 optimizes network identity management, solves identity scaling limits, and enables sub-second provisioning to power high-density, large-scale AI agent workloads. A common scale challenge: network identity management Operating with massive concurrency introduces fascinating new engineering challenges, particularly in how you manage network identities. Traditionally, custom controllers and workload orchestrators often assign unique, dynamic labels to each pod (such as agent-id, timestamps, or claim-uid). GKE Dataplane V2 , powered by eBPF technology, helps enforce robust network security policies by mapping pod labels to a numeric identity. Because agentic workflows generate highly unique labels for every pod, the system proactively provisions a distinct identity for each sandbox. In a rapidly changing environment, this serial allocation process can briefly pause pod creation as the system securely updates eBPF maps, occasionally leading to slower-than-desired initialization. Additionally, sophisticated workloads can approach the cluster-wide limit of 65,536 network identities, either through this rapid generation or overall scale of the workload itself. GKE network dataplane innovations for an agentic world Providing a reliable and highly secure platform is fundamental to everything we do. As such, we needed to find a way to provide the same underlying identity and security controls while providing higher scalability and performance. That's where the architectural innovations in GKE Dataplane V2 come in. A customer has testified to the success of Agent Substrate on GKE to orchestrate hundreds of thousands of secure environments across clusters and handle spikes of over 30,000 sandboxes on a single cluster. To achieve this, GKE relies on a two-pronged networking approach: Migrating high-cardinality data Google's GKE Dataplane V2 separates "identifying" data from "functional" metadata. Ensure your fields that do not actively participate in service selector matching or core resource grouping are migrated from the Pod's Labels set to the Annotations set. GKE Dataplane V2 intelligently calculates network identities based on labels rather than annotations, moving this high-cardinality metadata out of the labels completely bypasses the need for per-Pod identity generation. This elegant shift natively resolves identity scaling limits without sacrificing visibility. Advanced Cilium label filtering In addition, applying precise label exclusion filters (e.g., using the cilium-config-emergency-override ConfigMap in kube-system ) by configuring rules like !agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-name-hash or !timestamp , these explicitly instruct GKE Dataplane V2 to gracefully ignore these dynamic labels during security identity calculation. This means that even if a developer framework inadvertently introduces high-cardinality labels, configuring appropriate exclusion filters allows Google’s network dataplane to drop them automatically. As a result, identical agent types continue sharing a single Cilium pod identity, maintaining the ultra-low-latency startup times critical for dynamic AI workloads. By preventing linear identity growth and avoiding Cilium’s 65,536 identity limit, GKE provides leading speed and efficiency for fully isolated agents with 300 sandboxes per second at sub-second latency. Looking ahead For workloads that require extreme performance, scale, and density, Agent Substrate natively integrates these GKE Dataplane V2 recommendations while bypassing Kubernetes scheduling limits, pushing GKE’s performance and scale even further. In benchmark validation running 200,000 agents, Agent Substrate sustained 500 activations per second at less than 500 ms suspend and resume latency. You can deploy it on your existing GKE clusters today to minimize idle compute costs for your most demanding AI workflows. By optimizing network identity calculation and filtering high-cardinality metadata, GKE Dataplane V2 addresses critical infrastructure bottlenecks in large-scale AI workloads. These architectural improvements reduce sandbox provisioning latency to sub-second levels, minimize expensive GPU idle times, and help maintain high compute density. Ultimately, these efficiencies let you scale your agentic AI operations reliably while controlling operational costs. To learn more, explore Agent Sandbox and Agent Substrate on GKE.

title: Step into a new dimension with XREAL AURA, the first-of-its-kind wired XR glasses
raw_text: The world of work is rapidly evolving, and with it, the tools we use to stay productive and connected. As AI adoption transforms daily workflows, form factors like XR headsets and glasses offer fresh ways to reimagine how productive work happens across apps and devices. Today marks the launch of XREAL AURA , a first-of-kind set of wired XR glasses built on Android XR. An optical-see-through display with a 70-degree field of view that layers rich visual content directly onto your physical world, allowing you to stay connected. A glasses frame weight of less than 95g, allowing for extended work sessions by employees. Most importantly, AURA brings unique productivity benefits to users. Employees will have out-of-the-box support for enterprise apps, including popular titles currently available on the Google Play Store. And if the hundreds of Android productivity titles aren’t enough, you can also connect your laptop and bring those applications into your spatial environment as well. AURA’s displayport-in (DP-in) function makes it seamless to connect laptops across platforms directly alongside Android apps. Management and security of Android XR devices are crucial for IT teams. We introduced Android Enterprise management on Android XR earlier this year, and XREAL AURA devices will be managed through the same framework. Key management and security features include: Managed Google Play: Securely distribute and manage public and private business apps, to ensure that end users have all the tools they need. Android zero-touch enrollment: Automatically deploy Android devices remotely out-of-the-box, to save time and enable enrollment at scale. Device management: Support of fully managed device mode, to support configuration of core system resources like Wi-Fi, as well the ability to set system policies like disallowing apps. Google Play Protect: Defend against threats with proactive machine-learning powered detection of malware, phishing and ransomware. Core Android platform security: Multi-layered protections spanning from hardware to OS, with verified boot, and device encryption that keep devices protected from emerging threats with regular and modular security updates from Google. Device Trust from Android Enterprise: Secures devices, respects privacy, and empowers employees to work from anywhere, including devices that may not be managed. XREAL AURA allows users to easily see both the world around them as well as digital data at the same time. Because of its unique form factor, users can seamlessly switch between extended reality and interacting with their physical space. This unlocks new use cases for enterprise users that include: Offering spatial productivity across virtual monitors visible only to the user and with 3D content Getting help from virtual experts while working on a piece of equipment Easily visualizing complex information on top of physical spaces Designing and simulating products in 3D Using voice to easily guide information from the physical world into digital systems of record Android XR brings advanced computing and AI to daily work through powerful devices like the XREAL AURA wired glasses, all seamlessly managed by the secure and familiar Android Enterprise framework. title: Introducing VMware solution on Google Cloud
raw_text: Many organizations with workloads on VMware are looking for ways to expedite their data center exits, migrate and modernize their mission-critical workloads, or simply leverage the cloud as a secondary disaster recovery site. But they want to do so without altering existing operational playbooks. title: Powering the agentic enterprise with latest innovations in Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud
raw_text: For decades, core enterprise operations — from global supply chains and financial ledgers to billing engines — have relied on the performance and transactional integrity of Oracle databases. Today at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, Google Cloud and Oracle are expanding our partnership across the AI stack — spanning AI compute and infrastructure (including making Google TPUs available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure), enterprise data, and agentic AI — by deepening the integration between Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud, Google’s Agentic Data Cloud , and Gemini. By unifying Oracle’s mission-critical operational data and applications with Google Cloud’s data and AI ecosystem — including BigQuery and Gemini models — enterprises can move beyond static analytics and build autonomous, agentic workflows. This architecture breaks down traditional data silos, giving agents direct, secure, and real-time access to the foundational enterprise data required to drive real-world action. Foundational building blocks for agentic AI To unlock production-grade agentic AI, enterprises need more than raw model capability — they need strong database connectivity, unified data governance, and rich semantic context working together as a cohesive foundation. First announced at Google Cloud Next '26, the following core capabilities serve as the building blocks for building conversational intelligence, end-to-end governance, and autonomous agent environments on Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud: Remote MCP Server with Data API : The Remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server for Oracle workloads — powered by the IAM-governed ExecuteSQL Data API — is now generally available. Together, they provide a unified, standardized interface that enables AI agents, Google Cloud services, and enterprise applications to securely run SQL and interact directly with Oracle databases. By resolving database credentials automatically through Secret Manager and enforcing Google Cloud IAM policies, this capability eliminates the need for custom natural-language-to-SQL middleware, bastion VMs, or plaintext passwords. Knowledge Catalog integration : Google Cloud’s Knowledge Catalog integration, currently in preview, unifies enterprise metadata discovery and governance across Oracle databases and the broader Google Agentic Data Cloud. By automatically cataloging schemas and business metadata, organizations can enforce consistent access controls, track data provenance, and supply the rich semantic context that agents require to reason accurately over complex operational data. Click here to sign-up for this feature. Gemini connector for Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud Building directly on the foundational capabilities discussed above, we’re also announcing the preview of Gemini connector for Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud . With this native integration, business users and developers can interact directly with their Oracle databases on Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud using natural language queries right inside the Gemini app. Behind the scenes, Gemini automatically leverages Knowledge Catalog to discover, search, and ground responses strictly in the governed Oracle data each user is authorized to access — turning complex operational databases into an intuitive, conversational experience without compromising enterprise security. Click here to sign-up for this feature. Oracle in Gemini and Gemini in Oracle Beyond direct database queries, Google Cloud and Oracle are connecting agentic workflows across the broader application layer — bringing Oracle data into Gemini and embedding Gemini models natively inside Oracle applications: Oracle in Gemini: Available today, Oracle in Gemini introduces conversational analytics, cross-cloud database connectors, and domain-aware agents — including the new Oracle AI Database Agent in Gemini. Anchored by over 135 pre-built operational and developer skills and standardized MCP connectivity with zero plaintext credentials, enterprises can orchestrate multi-agent workflows across JD Edwards, E-Business Suite, NetSuite, and Oracle Fusion without custom SQL or brittle middleware. Gemini models in Oracle applications : Concurrently, Gemini frontier reasoning is embedded directly into Oracle Fusion AI Agent Studio , Fusion Claw , Oracle Fusion Applications, and NetSuite — combining Oracle database intelligence with Gemini’s agentic capabilities to automate execution across transactional systems of record. Partner-ready agentic blueprints: To help organizations rapidly deploy these governed workflows, Google Cloud and Oracle are collaborating with leading partners and global systems integrators — including Argano , Automus , Calfus , HCL , IBM , Infosys , LTM , Pythian , TCS , and Tessell — who provide pre-built operational skills, custom MCP connectors, and industry blueprints for production-grade agentic architectures. Empowering choice with lakehouse, streaming, and federation Every enterprise has distinct architectural priorities, latency thresholds, and governance requirements when connecting operational Oracle data to BigQuery and AI workloads. Rather than prescribing a one-size-fits-all integration pattern, Google Cloud and Oracle offer a complete spectrum of data unification choices so customers can select — or combine — the exact approach that best fits their workload and use case: Bi-directional Google Cloud borderless Lakehouse and Oracle AI Lakehouse Modern enterprise data architectures are increasingly multi-cloud and grounded in open standards. Building on our strategic partnership, Google Cloud and Oracle delivered a key innovation earlier this year to support cross-cloud data interoperability powered by open Apache Iceberg standard: integrating Google’s borderless Lakehouse with Oracle AI Lakehouse . This work enabled the borderless Lakehouse to read Apache Iceberg tables created by Oracle AI Lakehouse across any public cloud or on-premises environment, leveraging catalogs and storage supported by both platforms. Today, we are advancing it further by making it fully bi-directional with Oracle Access to Google Cloud borderless Lakehouse (preview) . Now, Oracle Autonomous AI Database and Google’s borderless Lakehouse (powered by BigQuery and Managed Spark) can directly query and execute write/DML operations on shared Apache Iceberg tables in Google Cloud Storage, completely eliminating the need for ETL or data replication. By utilizing a Lakehouse runtime REST catalog integrated into Oracle via DBMS_CATALOG , this bi-directional integration delivers an open-standards storage framework while empowering analytical teams (using BigQuery and Gemini) and operational teams (using Oracle SQL) to collaborate over a single, unified source of truth. You can click here to sign-up for this feature. Sub-second CDC streaming with OCI GoldenGate For organizations that prefer to continuously reflect mission-critical operational data inside BigQuery for high-scale analytics and AI, real-time change data capture (CDC) provides an immediate competitive edge. Through native OCI GoldenGate integration , CDC events are extracted directly from Oracle redo logs without touching table blocks or adding overhead to transactional workloads. Transactions stream securely across Google Cloud private networks straight into BigQuery managed tables, delivering sub-second analytical freshness to power Gemini, feature stores, and live business intelligence dashboards, while also streamlining migrations from on-premises environments to Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud. BigQuery query federation with Oracle When workloads call for on-demand operational visibility or infrequent cross-estate joins without moving data, BigQuery query federation with Oracle, in preview, enables real-time, in-place analytics directly against live Oracle databases. Using the EXTERNAL_QUERY function, data teams can execute native Oracle SQL directly from BigQuery queries, dashboards, and pipelines to retrieve live transactional records and join them easily with petabyte-scale BigQuery datasets. This zero-copy approach simplifies operations and lowers Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) by eliminating duplicate storage and ETL maintenance for ad-hoc lookups, intraday risk reporting, and live fraud detection. Please reach out to your Google Cloud account team if you want to sign-up for this feature. Operating inside a FedRAMP High-authorized environment enables federal agencies to safeguard sensitive, unclassified data while co-locating Oracle workloads with existing applications and Gemini. Agencies can access live Oracle data with minimal latency, streamlined billing, and simplified procurement via Google Cloud Marketplace or certified partners — all within their compliance boundaries. Building the agentic future By combining Oracle’s proven transactional engine with Google’s Agentic Data Cloud, enterprise data transitions from passive systems of record into an active, intelligent operational engine. Whether unifying data through open Apache Iceberg lakehouses, streaming sub-second changes via GoldenGate, federating live queries from BigQuery, or conversing directly with governed Oracle data through Gemini, organizations now have the complete flexibility and security required to deploy autonomous AI agents at scale — driving predictive insights and automated actions across their most critical business processes. Get started today Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud is available directly through the Google Cloud Marketplace , allowing you to deploy using your existing Google Cloud commitments, unified billing, and Oracle Support Rewards. To explore further, visit the Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud overview , dive into the official Oracle Database@Google Cloud Documentation , or reach out to your Google Cloud account team to schedule an architecture briefing.

title: Securely connecting Gemini Enterprise to Snowflake data
raw_text:
Enterprise AI needs to go beyond simple chat interfaces. To provide real value, AI agents must access your data warehouses to generate actionable insights, all while maintaining strict security and data governance. This guide explores how to build a secure bridge between Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise and Snowflake. By using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK), you can empower your agent to act as an assistant that understands natural language, generates precise SQL via Snowflake Cortex and executes queries with user-level permissions. Choosing the right integration pattern Direct Connection vs. custom orchestration The Google ADK architecture demonstrated in this post represents the advanced / custom orchestration pattern. It is designed for developers building complex, multi-agent systems on Google Cloud, such as workflows that combine Snowflake insights with external enterprise tools, custom reasoning loops, or cross-platform state management in Gemini Agent Engine. For standard enterprise basic use cases where you want to connect Gemini Enterprise directly to Snowflake use the joint solutions mentioned in this link . The architectural approach This architecture allows a business user to ask questions like, "What were our top 5 selling items in Texas last quarter?" Rather than exposing raw SQL execution to the client, the agent delegates both query generation and execution to a governed Snowflake Cortex Agent exposed through the Snowflake MCP server: Governed translation : The ADK agent passes the user's natural language question to the Snowflake MCP server, which invokes the Cortex Agent (CORTEX_AGENT_RUN) backed by Cortex Analyst semantic view. Direct execution within the governed boundary : The Cortex Agent translates the question into SQL and executes it directly inside Snowflake using the authenticated user's OAuth session and role privileges, returning the structured results to the ADK agent. This approach provides deterministic text-to-SQL translation mapped to your corporate semantic definitions, keeps query execution inside Snowflake's governed boundary, and reduces the risk of schema hallucinations or unvalidated SQL execution. System architecture flow The diagram below illustrates the trust boundaries and the numbered flow of execution between the Gemini Enterprise app and Snowflake ecosystems. Detailed execution sequence To highlight how the agent delegates natural language query translation and governed execution to the Snowflake Cortex Agent over MCP, see the sequence diagram below: Step 1: Setting up the Snowflake security integration A major risk in enterprise AI is granting the model broad access via a generic service account, which could allow users to bypass security restrictions. We solve this by using OAuth 2.0 to perform user impersonation. First, establish a confidential OAuth client in Snowflake to protect the client secret. The snippet below configures the security integration inside Snowflake: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN; 
CREATE OR REPLACE SECURITY INTEGRATION <SECURITY_INTEGRATION_NAME> 
TYPE = OAUTH 
ENABLED = TRUE 
OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM 
OAUTH_CLIENT_TYPE = 'CONFIDENTIAL' 
-- Google Cloud's official handshake receiver address: 
OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI = 'https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/oauth-redirect' 
OAUTH_ISSUE_REFRESH_TOKENS = TRUE 
-- Let the connection stay alive for 90 days (max Snowflake allowed limit) 
OAUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_VALIDITY = 7776000;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2519db8890>)])]> To retrieve the generated client credentials needed for the Google Cloud configuration, run the following command in Snowflake: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Retrieve OAuth Client ID and Client Secret
SELECT SYSTEM$SHOW_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRETS('<SECURITY_INTEGRATION_NAME>');"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2519f06550>)])]> Step 2: Data governance and access control Apply the principle of least privilege by creating a dedicated role for your agent inside Snowflake. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN;
-- 1. Create a dedicated role
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
GRANT ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME> TO USER <BUSINESS_USER_NAME>; 
USE ROLE SYSADMIN;
-- 2. Grant structural access
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE <DATABASE_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
-- 3. Grant compute access
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE <WAREHOUSE_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
-- 4 .Grant access to the semantic layer
GRANT SELECT, REFERENCES ON SEMANTIC VIEW <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SEMANTIC_VIEW_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
-- 5. Grant select privileges on underlying raw data tables
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2519f07150>)])]> IMPORTANT The user context must have SELECT privileges on the physical tables backing the semantic view. Granting access only to the semantic view will cause runtime errors during query execution. If granting direct access to base tables is not permitted by your security policy, place a Snowflake Secure View over the physical tables and build the Semantic View on top of it. Because Snowflake views execute with Owner's Rights , the user's GenAI role only needs SELECT privileges on the Secure View and Semantic View rather than the raw tables. Snowflake OAuth tokens capture and bind to the user's DEFAULT_ROLE and DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE at the exact moment of authorization. If a user authorizes the connection before these defaults are configured, the session will be locked to the wrong role(role available at that time) and query execution will fail if the intended role will not have required privileges. Set defaults(as shown below) prior to authorizing in Gemini Enterprise. Authorize connection: Have the user perform the one-time OAuth authorization in Gemini Enterprise. (Optional) Revert defaults: Once authorized, the user can safely revert their default role and warehouse in Snowflake back to their standard operational preferences. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "ALTER USER <BUSINESS_USER_NAME> SET DEFAULT_ROLE = '<GENAI_ROLE_NAME>';
ALTER USER <BUSINESS_USER_NAME> SET DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE = '<WAREHOUSE_NAME>';"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2519e18110>)])]> Step 3: Provisioning the Cortex Agent and MCP server inside Snowflake Next, create a governed Cortex Agent in Snowflake using your semantic view, then provision an MCP server that exposes the agent via the CORTEX_AGENT_RUN tool type. This approach delegates both SQL generation and query execution to Snowflake while enforcing the caller's OAuth identity and role permissions. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'USE DATABASE <DATABASE_NAME>;
USE SCHEMA <SCHEMA_NAME>;
USE ROLE SYSADMIN;

-- 1. Create the Cortex Agent over your semantic view
CREATE OR REPLACE AGENT <AGENT_NAME>
 COMMENT = 'Governed data assistant for business queries'
 PROFILE = '{"cortex_analyst": {"semantic_models": ["<DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SEMANTIC_VIEW_NAME>"]}}';

-- 2. Provision the MCP Server exposing the Cortex Agent
CREATE OR REPLACE MCP SERVER <SERVER_NAME>
FROM SPECIFICATION $$
tools:
 - name: "run_cortex_agent"
 type: "CORTEX_AGENT_RUN"
 identifier: "<DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<AGENT_NAME>"
 title: "Cortex Agent Assistant"
 description: "Converts natural language questions into SQL and executes them directly within Snowflake using the caller's OAuth session permissions."
$$;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2519d57290>)])]> ISOLATION & GOVERNANCE NOTE: By using CORTEX_AGENT_RUN, query generation and execution remain fully contained within Snowflake's governed security boundary. Avoid exposing raw execution tools like SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL to external clients, as doing so introduces unnecessary security surface area and bypasses centralized Cortex Agent governance. Step 4: Locating and constructing the MCP server URL The ADK code requires the endpoint URL of your Snowflake-managed MCP server. Now that the server is provisioned, you must first grant access to the server, and then you can retrieve its exact endpoint URL using the following query in a Snowflake worksheet: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '-- 1. Grant access to the Cortex Agent and the MCP server

GRANT USAGE ON AGENT <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<AGENT_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
GRANT USAGE ON MCP SERVER <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SERVER_NAME> TO ROLE <GENAI_ROLE_NAME>;
-- 2. View the MCP URL
DESCRIBE MCP SERVER <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SERVER_NAME>;
-- Or:
DESC MCP SERVER <DATABASE_NAME>.<SCHEMA_NAME>.<SERVER_NAME>;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f25199aeb50>)])]> In the command output, inspect the metadata properties to locate the endpoint link. The URL is structured as follows: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'https://<org_name>-<account_name>.snowflakecomputing.com/api/v2/databases/<database_name>/schemas/<schema_name>/mcp-servers/<server_name>'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f25199ae290>)])]> Step 5: Connecting via Google ADK With the MCP Server created and its URL resolved, write your agent code using the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK). In your Python code, define the unique identifier AUTH_ID (e.g. snowflake_oauth_conn) that the agent will use to extract user credentials. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'import os
import re
from typing import Optional
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import LlmAgent
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.mcp_toolset import McpToolset
from google.adk.tools.mcp_tool.mcp_session_manager import StreamableHTTPConnectionParams
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext

# Define the Auth ID first in your code. 
# You will use this exact name when registering the agent in the Google Cloud Console.
# Gemini Enterprise maps the authorization token to this identifier in the ToolContext.
AUTH_ID = "snowflake_oauth_conn" 

# 1. OAuth Header Extraction:
# Define a callback to dynamically extract the user's OAuth token injected by Gemini Enterprise 
# and generate the Authorization headers required to authenticate with the Snowflake MCP.
def get_auth_headers(tool_context: Optional[ToolContext] = None) -> dict: 
 """ 
 OAuth Handling Callback: Dynamically extracts the user's OAuth token injected by Gemini Enterprise and generates the headers required to authenticate with the Snowflake MCP. 
 """ 
 token = None 
 if tool_context and hasattr(tool_context, "state"): 
 try: 
 # Parse the state dictionary injected by Gemini Enterprise containing authorization states 
 state_dict = tool_context.state.to_dict() if hasattr(tool_context.state, 'to_dict') else tool_context.state 
 pattern = re.compile(fr".*{re.escape(AUTH_ID)}.*", re.IGNORECASE) 
 # Find the active token matching our Auth ID (snowflake_oauth_conn)
 matching_keys = [k for k in state_dict.keys() if pattern.match(k)] 
 if matching_keys: 
 token = state_dict.get(matching_keys[0]) 
 except Exception as e: 
 print(f"Warning: Failed to read ToolContext OAuth state: {e}") 
 # Return authorization headers. If token is None, requests to MCP will fail.
 return { 
 "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}", 
 "Content-Type": "application/json", 
 "Accept": "application/json, text/event-stream", 
 } 

# 2. MCP Initialization:
# Define the Snowflake MCP URL retrieved from 'DESCRIBE MCP SERVER' directly in the code:
MCP_SERVER_URL = "<YOUR_MCP_SERVER_URL>" # Replace with the URL retrieved from 'DESCRIBE MCP SERVER' 

# Initialize the Snowflake MCP Toolset using this URL.
snowflake_mcp = McpToolset( 
 connection_params=StreamableHTTPConnectionParams( 
 url=MCP_SERVER_URL 
 ), 
 header_provider=get_auth_headers
) 

# 3. Build the Agent:
# Construct the LlmAgent using the Gemini 2.5 Flash model and attach the Snowflake MCP Toolset.
root_agent = LlmAgent( 
 model="gemini-2.5-flash", 
 name="enterprise_data_analyst", 
 instruction=( 
 "You are an enterprise data analyst. Use the `enterprise_data_agent` tool " 
 "on the Snowflake MCP server to answer business questions. Pass the user's " 
 "natural language question to the tool, which translates it into SQL and " 
 "executes it directly within Snowflake's governed boundary, then present " 
 "the results clearly to the user." 
 ), 
 tools=[snowflake_mcp]
)'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f25199ac250>)])]> NOTE: The Python snippet above represents a plain/vanilla version of the agent setup. Depending on your organization's specific requirements, you should add robustness on top of this template (e.g., custom error handling, structured schemas, custom prompts, configurations, and additional tool wrappers). title: Scale agents securely with IAM Helper Agent Skills and MCP Tools
raw_text: As organizations adopt autonomous agents to build applications, securing identities and access has become more challenging. Developers relying on agents to provision cloud resources, write Terraform, and deploy microservices at machine-speed only find their CI/CD pipelines blo cked even faster as security friction scales. To help you get ahead of agentic-era Identity and Access Management, today we’re introducing IAM Helper. This suite of intelligent, agent-facing building blocks can automate complex, end-to-end IAM workflows. As an agent-native orchestration and interface layer for Google Cloud IAM, it augments Google Cloud’s core IAM engines — including Policy Intelligence and Privileged Access Manager (PAM) — making IAM skills callable directly by autonomous code assistants, deployment pipelines, and custom agents. Using this functionality reduces the administrative overhead of maintaining least-privilege security and agent governance, while maximizing utility, and accelerating deployment. IAM Helper Agent Skills: Fast, secure deployment with automated governance Manual troubleshooting of permission blockers creates friction for engineering and administrators, while shortcuts can lead to broad agent over-permissioning that puts least privilege at risk. IAM Helper empowers agents to handle access management dynamically. It shifts the burden of policy evaluation away from human administrators and LLMs, offloading complex orchestration directly to the Google Cloud backend, to maximize token efficiency and prevent costly operational bottlenecks. Rather than operating as isolated utilities, IAM Helper Agent Skills guide agents through the cloud access lifecycle. These end-to-end workflows, helper scripts, and guardrails packaged using the open Agent Skills standard can orchestrate multiple underlying functions and APIs to resolve complex IAM tasks. They work across common agents (Gemini CLI, Gemini Cloud Assist, ADK, Claude Code, and Cursor). Built-in guardrails and real-world impact Every IAM Helper agent skill separates read-only discovery from policy changes: Diagnostics and simulations run automatically, while any change to access policies pauses for human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmation based on customizable risk tiers. To see the value of IAM Helper in practice, consider how it transforms two everyday scenarios: Scaled user-assisted remediation : Suppose a developer's coding agent hits a 403 error while deploying a new application. Rather than filing a support ticket and idling, the agent uses iam-helper-for-troubleshooting to identify the missing Pub/Sub permission in seconds, then uses iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management to request a one-hour JIT grant, eliminating hours of debugging friction. Autonomous pipeline self-healing : An infrastructure agent encounters a permission block during a routine deployment pipeline. Rather than failing the build, the pipeline uses IAM Helper Agent skills to generate a revised, least-privilege policy, verifies against 90 days of logs via iam-helper-for-policy-simulator that active services won't break, and routes the change to an admin for quick approval. IAM Helper Agent Skills are designed for maximum token and cost efficiency, allowing agents to execute multi-step administrative operations autonomously. Authoring compliant, least-privilege policies : As DevOps engineers translate access requirements into JSON, YAML, or Terraform HCL, iam-helper-for-policy-management generates and validates IAM v1 allow bindings and IAM v2 deny rules. It automatically catches and blocks risky configs before they are applied, including public access (allUsers) and broad basic roles (roles/owner, roles/editor). It adapts to the user’s role: Developers can check if they can unblock themselves locally or generate a structured ticket for their administrator (Requester flow), while security administrators can trace inherited allow and v2 deny rules across organization, folder, and project hierarchies to resolve the issue (Resolver flow). Simulating blast radius before rolling out changes : Before a platform engineer updates a policy or applies IAM Recommender role reductions, they need confidence that active workloads won't break. iam-helper-for-policy-simulator walks the agent through a structured plan, simulate, analyze, and apply flow, testing proposed changes against 90 days of historical access logs to confirm existing traffic won't be disrupted before any update takes effect. Elevating access just-in-time instead of granting standing privileges : When responders or maintenance agents need temporary production access, iam-helper-for-privileged-access-management manages the lifecycle of on-demand credentials through Privileged Access Manager (PAM). It supports requester, administrator, and approver workflows so elevated access is audited, time-bound, and automatically revoked once the task is done. While IAM Helper Agent Skills supply the high-level workflow logic, they are all based on a common set of foundational MCP Tools. Powered by Google Cloud IAM MCP tools Google Cloud IAM Helper MCP tools provide the backend connection through atomic, read-only functions exposed via Google-managed MCP servers across core IAM endpoints (Policy Troubleshooter, Policy Analyzer, Policy Simulator, and IAM v1/v2 APIs). Rather than requiring teams to write custom API wrappers, MCP tools give agents a standard way to query the cloud backend and get exact answers without parsing verbose policy documents in the prompt, maximizing token efficiency. Agents can dynamically discover and invoke these tools to execute basic operations like checking permissions or listing roles when custom logic is required. Because operations like hierarchy traversal, group expansion, and policy evaluation happen on dedicated IAM endpoints (spanning IAM v1 allow roles, IAM v2 deny, Policy Troubleshooter, and Policy Analyzer), skills run quickly and accurately with minimal token usage. Teams can also use these atomic MCP tools directly when writing their own custom Agent Skills, making it straightforward to combine Google Cloud's IAM capabilities with internal ticketing systems, custom compliance checks, and existing deployment pipelines. Start building with IAM Helper Agent skills today by exploring our Google Cloud Agent Skills Catalog and dive deeper with the official IAM documentation .

title: Bringing Google TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
raw_text: As AI workloads scale across every industry, organizations need compute options that optimize throughput, latency, and unit economics across the AI lifecycle. To meet this demand, Oracle and Google Cloud are partnering to bring Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), making OCI the first hyperscaler outside Google to offer TPUs. Together, we will deploy TPU capacity on OCI starting in the calendar year 2027. TPUs: Co-designed from silicon to software Google built its first TPU more than ten years ago on a clear product thesis: co-designing custom silicon alongside optical networking, power delivery, liquid cooling, and compiler software yields gains in performance per watt and total cost of ownership that isolated components cannot match. TPU v1 delivered 30x the throughput per watt of contemporary processors. Today, TPUs train and serve Gemini across Google's billion-user products, and the eighth-generation TPUs deliver up to 12.6 PFLOPS of native FP4 compute per chip, over 100x TPU v1's 92 TFLOPS at up to 2x the performance per watt of the previous generation. However, raw FLOPS alone do not determine customer economics across training and inference. For training, the governing metric is goodput; the percentage of time a cluster spends doing productive computation. For inference, the governing metrics are latency and cost per token. TPUs address both through system-level co-design. By pairing on-die Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) routing with Optical Circuit Switching (OCS), the control plane detects hardware or link degradations and dynamically routes optical paths around faults in real time without job restarts, sustaining over 97% goodput across thousands of chips on large-scale training runs and high availability for production serving. Increased on-chip SRAM, more HBM capacity, and a new low-diameter interconnect topology that cuts network hops by more than 50% allow the latest generation TPUs to deliver up to 80% better performance per dollar for low-latency serving. This hardware efficiency translates into product velocity when developers can adopt it without friction. Our recent announcements at the PyTorch Conference reinforce our commitment to making the Google TPU software ecosystem an open, developer-friendly environment for the PyTorch community. Notably, TorchTPU, our native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, is now available as open source on GitHub. You can now train, serve, and deploy models on TPUs using the tools you already rely on, including vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, Ray, TorchRec, Hugging Face, LiteRT. This portability lets teams assign each workload to the accelerator that delivers the lowest cost per token or fastest time to train, without rewriting model code. And with today’s announcement, they will soon be able to assign those workloads to TPUs on Google Cloud or Oracle infrastructure. Expanding the AI infrastructure ecosystem with OCI Even as TPU adoption on Google Cloud grows, the global demand for AI compute exceeds any single cloud provider's footprint.Bringing TPUs to OCI gives customers four distinct benefits: Data centers engineered for AI density: Google's TPU systems are designed for direct liquid cooling at rack scale, and OCI's next-generation data centers are built for exactly that profile. Oracle delivers flexible, durable capacity that can shift between frontier model training and production inference as customer demand changes. Pairing TPU efficiency with Oracle’s innovative power and cooling approaches, helps bring energy-efficient AI-compute capacity online rapidly, and at global scale. Secure, high-performance networking with Oracle Acceleron: While TPUs move chip-to-chip traffic over ICI and OCS, Oracle Acceleron provides the networking foundation that connects TPU capacity to the rest of OCI. Acceleron’s SmartNIC with hardware-level tenant isolation, High Performance Fabric, and Zero Trust Packet Routing moves data between Oracle databases, storage, and TPU clusters with high throughput and low latency, without taxing host compute and without weakening security boundaries. Proximity to enterprise data: Oracle databases are often the system-of-record for enterprise organizations. Offering TPUs directly within OCI lets organizations run fine-tuning and inference next to their existing enterprise data without costly cross-cloud transfers. Multi-architecture choice: Providing TPUs alongside GPUs inside OCI gives teams the flexibility to assign each AI workload stage to the optimal accelerator for cost and performance. By bringing Google TPUs to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Google Cloud and Oracle are opening up over a decade of purpose-built AI systems engineering to a broader ecosystem of builders. When customers have more choices of purpose-built compute across more clouds, the entire industry builds faster and operates more efficiently. We can’t wait to see what you build.
